catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress seems to be predictably assigned to the last vowel of the stem or first vowel of suffixes on stems with no vowel. Adverbs take penultimate stress. But there are exceptions to these rules. There are some contrasts for tone: pää [pɑɑ́] 'bird sp.' ... pää [pɑ̀ɑ] 'body' ... agana [ə̀ɡənə] 'sky' ... agana [əɡə́nə] 'lid' ... Beyond that we have little knowledge of the tone system.

[…] Generally, accent is placed on the final vowel of the stem […] in nouns (10) and in verbs (11), though there are many exceptions to this generalization. [p. 15:] If there is no vowel in the stem of a noun or adjective, the accent falls on the first vowel of the suffix. […] When the last segment of the stem is a mid-central vowel, the accent falls on the rightmost non-mid-central vowel (15), unless all the vowels in the stem are /ə/ (16), in which case it falls on the final vowel of the stem.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (from Whitney 1992 OPD: 'Stress seems to be predictably assigned to the last vowel of the stem or first vowel of suffixes on stems with no vowel'), so it agrees on the set by morphology / stem-final classification; it adds the schwa-avoidance sub-rules, prefix/suffix accent shifts, compound secondary accent, the three pitch-contrast pairs, and drops the OPD's 'adverbs take penultimate stress' clause (not mentioned here). Where the OPD said 'some contrasts for tone', this says pitch is contrastive 'in some environments' but 'not productive in the language as a whole'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (high pitch + loudness, sometimes length) falls on the final vowel of the stem in nouns and verbs; if the stem has no vowel, on the first vowel of the suffix. Refinements: if the stem ends in schwa, accent goes to the rightmost non-schwa vowel of the stem; if all stem vowels are schwa, to the final stem vowel; the first syllable is accented when all later nuclei are schwa or when the stem is all schwa with no final stem vowel. Imperfective n- and gnomic nə- prefixed verbs accent the suffix; perfective ə- prefixed verbs accent the prefix. Affixation shifts accent: the transitivizer m(ə)- pulls it left, a set of suffixes (-nə, -nu, -we, -ma, -ijə, -ikə) pull it right. Pitch is contrastive only marginally (three singular/plural pairs, Table 13) and 'not productive in the language as a whole'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 15: 'In compound words, primary accent falls on the stem of the first word, secondary accent on the accented syllable of the second word, as in 14.' Also p. 30: stress on the root of the first element of compound verbs; p. 33: the authors would have to explain why 'secondary stress would fall on an epenthesized vowel' in some forms.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 14: 'though there are many exceptions to this generalization'; the schwa-conditioned and prefix-conditioned cases above are given as sub-rules; p. 33 fn: one word ['ɔk.wɪ] 'black palm' contrasts in stress with [ɔk'wɪ] 'to good' (same segments).
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe the Akoye of Waikuna village, Albert Mountains south-west of Kanabea (Grammar Essentials p. 1: fieldwork May 1983-July 1991 'mostly in Waikuna village'); the Phonology Essentials notes one variant form from 'the Pipo area' (p. 16) but describes no separate dialect.

audit.recode_to: Keep classification morphological (stem-final accent). Re-cite to Whitney & Whitney 2000 §3.5.1 pp. 14-16 and refine the primary-stress rule: accent (high pitch + loudness) on the final stem vowel in nouns and verbs; stemless nouns/adjectives and IMPF/GNOM-prefixed verbs accent the first suffix vowel, PF a- prefixed verbs accent the prefix; /ə/ is skipped (accent on rightmost non-mid-central stem vowel; initial syllable if all later nuclei are /ə/); transitivizer ma- pulls accent left and several suffixes pull it right; 'many exceptions'; pitch contrastive only in a few noun pairs. Drop the hedge-based caution ('seems') since the 2000 source states the rule without it; the OPD's 'adverbs penultimate' line is not repeated in 2000 and should be attributed to the OPD only.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding OPD passage is verbatim on p. 3 of the held at the stated lines. (2) The deciding source is a 1992 SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (5 pp., one hedged sentence on stress). Glottolog lists only Whitney & Whitney 1991 Grammar Essentials; SIL-PNG also published Whitney & Whitney 2000 Akoye Phonology Essentials (48 pp.), which is the best available account. (3) Both downloaded now via the Internet Archive (sil.org is could not be reached by automated download): the 2000 Phonology Essentials §3.5.1 confirms the stem-final morphological accent rule and refines it (schwa avoidance, prefix accent in perfective forms, accent-attracting affixes, compounds, 'many exceptions', marginal pitch contrast); the 1991 grammar's phonology overview is silent on stress placement.
